Sequential Check for a Budget Constrained K-Population Contrast

Source: R/seq_budget.R
seq_budget.Rd

Given the data collected so far from each of K populations, the cost of an observation in each, and a total budget, reports whether sampling should continue under the sequential procedure of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025), and returns the current estimate of the contrast with its confidence interval. Use it when a contrast of means has to be estimated as precisely as a fixed budget allows and the population variances that determine the best allocation are unknown. seq_budget_next says which group the next observation should come from.

Usage

seq_budget(
  groups,
  contrast_weights,
  cost_per_group,
  budget,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  closed = NULL
)

Arguments

groups

A list of K (at least 2) numeric vectors, one per population, holding the observations collected so far. Each needs at least 2 observations, so that a sample variance exists, and no missing or infinite values. The groups may have different sizes.

contrast_weights

Numeric vector of length K giving the contrast coefficients \(c_i\), in the order of groups, not all zero. Code the contrast so that larger values are better if a noninferiority or superiority decision is planned. The article takes the weights to sum to zero; the sum is not checked.

cost_per_group

Numeric vector of length K giving the cost \(a_i\) of one observation from each population, each positive, in the same units as budget and in the order of groups.

budget

The total budget \(A_0\) for all observations, the pilot included: a single positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level of the two-sided interval (default 0.95). It plays no part in the decision functions, which take a one-sided level of their own.

closed

Optional; leave NULL (the default) to judge every group on the current data. For the first passage rule, a logical vector of length K that is TRUE for each group from which sampling has already stopped: the met_per_group attribute of the previous check. A closed group stays closed, unless its variance is unusable.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and six rows, in this order: lower_limit, contrast (the estimate \(\hat{\psi}\)), upper_limit, variance (the estimated variance \(\hat{V}\) of the contrast estimator), current_total_n, and current_total_cost. A group whose variance is unusable adds nothing to the variance row, so the two limits are then too close together and are not an interval to report (see Details). Its attributes are:

method

the label of the procedure, "budget constrained K-population contrast". The next observation and decision functions recognize the object by it.

is_satisfied, rule_met, budget_exhausted

the three stopping attributes described under Details.

budget_exceeded

TRUE when the data already cost more than the budget.

variance_unusable

TRUE when the sample variance of at least one group with a nonzero weight is unusable (zero, or computed from observations that agree to about ten significant digits); FALSE otherwise.

current_n, criterion_n

the totals over groups of the current sample sizes and of the criteria.

conf_level

the confidence level of the interval.

notes

a character vector with the notes that print() shows (empty when there are none).

n_per_group, mean_per_group, sd_per_group

the sample size, mean, and standard deviation of each group, in the order of groups.

target_per_group

the right hand side of Equation 18 for each group, not rounded.

criterion_per_group

the smallest whole number at or above each target, a target within one part in 1e10 above a whole number counting as that number (an integer vector); for a group whose variance is unusable, its current size plus one.

met_per_group

TRUE for each group that has met its criterion or, under the first passage rule, was closed earlier.

not_estimable_per_group

TRUE for each group with a nonzero weight whose variance is unusable.

cost_per_group, contrast_weights, budget

the inputs.

remaining_budget

the budget minus the current total cost; negative when the budget is exceeded.

Details

The criterion. The contrast \(\psi = \sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i \mu_i\) is estimated by \(\hat{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i \bar{X}_i\), whose variance is estimated by \(\hat{V} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i^2 s_i^2 / N_i\) (Equation 5 of the article with sample variances). The variance is smallest, for a budget \(A_0\) and unit costs \(a_i\), at the allocation of seq_budget_optimal, which depends on the unknown standard deviations. The sequential procedure substitutes the current sample standard deviations: group \(i\) has met its criterion when (Equation 18) $$N_i \ge \frac{A_0 \, |c_i| \, s_i} {\sqrt{a_i} \, \sum_{l=1}^{K} |c_l| \, s_l \, \sqrt{a_l}}.$$ The right hand side is stored unrounded as target_per_group; the smallest whole number that satisfies the inequality is criterion_per_group. As for every criterion sample size in the package, a target that exceeds a whole number by no more than one part in 1e10 is taken to be that number, so that representation error in a target that is a whole number does not add an observation. The interval is \(\hat{\psi} \pm z \sqrt{\hat{V}}\) with the standard normal quantile \(z\) for conf_level.

How close the coverage is to nominal. The coverage of the interval is asymptotic. In samples of realistic size it falls short of nominal, because the estimated variance runs below the true one, and the shortfall depends on the pilot size. In simulations with a pilot of 10 per group (the article's simulation setting) and a budget that bought about 40 to 100 observations per group, the 95 percent interval covered the contrast in 0.942 to 0.949 of studies for normal populations and 0.936 to 0.941 for skewed ones; with 15 to 30 per group the figures were 0.936 and 0.925. A pilot of 5 gave about the same with the larger budgets and somewhat less with the small one (0.931 and 0.907 in another set of runs), and the minimum pilot of 2 gave markedly less; seq_budget_pilot has those figures. seq_budget_sensitivity measures the coverage for a design of interest.

When sampling ends. Sampling ends when (a) every group has met its criterion or (b) the budget cannot pay for another needed observation (the article, p. 430). Three attributes state which:

rule_met

TRUE when every group with a nonzero weight has met its criterion.

budget_exhausted

TRUE when at least one group is still below its criterion and what is left of the budget cannot pay for one more observation from any such group. Only the groups that still need observations count: a cheaper group that has already met its criterion does not keep the procedure going.

is_satisfied

TRUE when sampling has ended, by (a) or by (b), and the variance of every group could be used. It is FALSE while sampling should continue. It is also FALSE whenever the variance of a group is unusable, which the attribute variance_unusable reports (see below).

The function seq_budget_next has no group to name, and returns NA, exactly when one of the first two attributes is TRUE; a loop that adds observations should end on that NA. Unless a variance is unusable, that is also exactly when is_satisfied is TRUE.

The targets of Equation 18 always cost exactly the budget in total (multiply each by its \(a_i\) and add). Judged on the current data, therefore, every group can be at or above its criterion without passing the budget only when each sample size equals its target exactly. So with the default closed = NULL the procedure nearly always ends by (b), with less of the budget left than the next needed observation costs and one or more groups still below their criteria. The printed object then carries a note that gives the amount left and names those groups, and its stopping line reads Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted), because the rule itself (every group at its criterion) was not met. is_satisfied is TRUE all the same: it says that sampling has ended. A fourth attribute, budget_exceeded, is TRUE when the data supplied already cost more than the budget (for example a pilot the budget cannot pay for); the result is then flagged with a note, because the budget constraint does not hold for it.

Two readings of "has met its criterion". In the article a population stops being sampled the first time it meets its criterion and is never sampled again (Stage 1 and Stage 2, pp. 429 to 430), and the open populations are visited one at a time, in rounds. A check sees only the current data, so by default it judges every group afresh: a group that met its criterion earlier and has since fallen below it, because the other standard deviations moved, is sampled again. This default is the package's choice, not the article's procedure. In simulations of three designs from Table 1 of the article (budget 5,000, pilot 10, normal and skewed populations) it left about 10 to 12 of the budget unspent where the first passage rule left 19 to 42, and the true variance of the estimator at the final sample sizes was 0.2 to 1.0 percent smaller; coverage differed by at most 0.006, in either direction. For the first passage rule, pass the met_per_group attribute of the previous check as closed, and ask seq_budget_next for order = "rounds"; the help page of that function lists the three respects in which the result still differs from the article's procedure. Under the first passage rule rule_met can become TRUE with part of the budget unspent.

A group whose variance is unusable. When the sample variance of a group with a nonzero weight is zero, no variance has been estimated for that group. As everywhere in the package when a variance estimate is unusable, the stopping rule is then reported as not met (rule_met and is_satisfied are FALSE), attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so; see smsd_check_methods. This happens when every observation in the group is the same, which a small pilot and coarsely scored data can produce, or the same to about ten significant digits, so that whatever variance is computed is rounding error. (Scores so large that a sample variance overflows are not this case: the function stops with a message that says to rescale them.) The group's share of the budget cannot be estimated and the variance of the contrast is understated; its target is reported as zero and its criterion as one more than its current size. The limits are still computed, from the understated variance, so they are too close together (when every group is constant both equal the estimate) and are not an interval to report. summary(), glance(), and tidy() return them without the note, so test attr(out, "variance_unusable") before using the limits. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the article, under which such a group has met its criterion (the right hand side of Equation 18 is zero) and is never sampled again, so that a pilot of equal scores would fix that group's variance at zero for the rest of the study.

seq_budget_next names such a group whenever no group whose variance can be used has fewer observations than it has, so it is sampled at the pace of the least sampled of the other groups until its observations differ. When the equal scores were an accident of a small pilot, one or two further observations usually settle the matter. A group that really is constant, or nearly so (a ceiling or a floor on the measure), keeps that pace for as long as its observations stay equal, which can be to the end of the study. It then receives about as many observations as the least sampled of the other groups, far more than its share when it is expensive, and the study ends with a variance that is still unusable. In a simulated example in which the most expensive of three groups scored at its ceiling 98 percent of the time, that group took 49 percent of the budget where its optimal share was 14 percent, the variance of the estimator was 1.6 times the optimum, and 61 percent of the studies ended with the group's variance still unusable. If a group shows no variation after more than a few observations beyond the pilot, stop and reconsider the measure before spending the rest of the budget.

Sampling still ends when the budget cannot pay for another observation: budget_exhausted is TRUE and seq_budget_next() returns NA. is_satisfied stays FALSE, the printed notes say why, and the decision functions refuse the check, because the interval rests on a variance of zero for at least one group. (For large scores that differ only far down their digits, subtracting the same constant from every score restores a usable variance; it leaves a contrast whose weights sum to zero unchanged.)

Names. groups, contrast_weights, and cost_per_group are matched by position. If more than one of them is named, the names must be the same and in the same order; otherwise the function stops, so that weights or costs named in another order (for example against a list made by split(), which is in alphabetical order) are not applied to the wrong groups.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Luh, W. M., & Guo, J. H. (2016). Sample size planning for the noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast with cost considerations. Psychological Methods, 21(1), 13–34. doi:10.1037/met0000039

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

See also

seq_budget_next for the next observation, seq_budget_pilot and seq_budget_optimal for planning, decide_seq_budget for the tests, and seq_budget_sensitivity for a simulation of a planned design. The vignette is vignette("seq-budget", package = "SMSD").

In DMAR, ss_seq_c is the sequential fixed-width interval for a contrast, and ss_aipe_c and equivalence_c are the fixed sample size cousins.

Other seq_budget: decide_seq_budget, seq_budget_next(), seq_budget_optimal(), seq_budget_pilot(), seq_budget_sensitivity()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Scores after a new training format (group 1) and two existing formats.
# An observation costs 38, 15, and 10, and the budget is 1,500.
set.seed(113)
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
costs <- c(38, 15, 10)
scores <- list(
  rnorm(10, mean = 52, sd = 9),
  rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6),
  rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6)
)
out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 1500)
out
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 30
#>   Criterion n     : 65
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -9.311685
#>   contrast          : -3.364913
#>   upper_limit       : 2.581859
#>   variance          : 9.205903
#>   current_total_n   : 30
#>   current_total_cost: 630
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
#> [1] 29 14 22
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
#> [1] 870

# Add one observation at a time, to the group seq_budget_next() names,
# until it has none to name. The cost never passes the budget.
true_means <- c(52, 50, 50)
true_sds <- c(9, 6, 6)
repeat {
  out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 1500)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], rnorm(1, true_means[g], true_sds[g]))
}
out
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 65
#>   Criterion n     : 67
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -3.175372
#>   contrast          : 0.5710176
#>   upper_limit       : 4.317407
#>   variance          : 3.653673
#>   current_total_n   : 65
#>   current_total_cost: 1499
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted)
#> 
#>   Note: Sampling has ended because the budget cannot pay for another
#>         observation: 1 of 1500 is left, and one more observation from a
#>         group still below its criterion (groups 2 and 3) costs at least
#>         10.
attr(out, "n_per_group")
#> [1] 28 13 24
